title: Walking and sitting together

segments.voice: Yesterday, sampajanna, walking in the city: normal pace, eyes open, the feet as the thread. Your line was every step, here. Did a stoplight become a bell? Day one hundred twenty-two, the last day of the walking week.

Sit. Walk. Sit. Walk. Sit. Lunch. Walk. Sit. That's a retreat schedule, the kind taped to the wall outside a meditation hall. It can look like somebody couldn't make up their mind. But on retreat, the walking isn't a break from the practice. After forty minutes on a cushion, the knees ache and the mind gets foggy. After forty minutes walking, the mind wants to settle down again. The two keep each other honest. Today, at the end of our walking week, we put them side by side.
screen: `SIT. WALK. SIT. WALK.` → `NOT A BREAK FROM PRACTICE.` → `THEY KEEP EACH OTHER HONEST.`

segments.voice: The pattern is old. In a discourse in the Numerical Discourses, the Buddha describes a monk who is devoted to wakefulness. By day, he says, the monk spends the time walking back and forth and sitting, clearing the mind of what gets in the way. In the first part of the night, the same: walking and sitting. In the middle of the night he lies down on his right side, like a resting lion, and sleeps, mindful of when to get up. In the last part of the night, walking and sitting again. Walking and sitting are named together, as one practice with two postures. Why pair them? Each covers the other's weak spot. Sitting is good for depth and stillness, but it can slide into sleepiness, which the texts call dullness, one of the five hindrances from last week. Walking wakes the body up and keeps you alert, but it can stay on the surface. So you sit until you start to fade, walk until you start to scatter, and sit again. Retreat schedules still follow that rhythm. Look back at the week and you'll see what you've collected. The lane: twenty or thirty paces with nowhere to get to. Lifting, moving, placing. The turn that counts too. The five blessings, including concentration that lasts. And the sidewalk, where every step can be here. Put that beside the sitting you learned before, and you have two ways of doing the same thing: staying with this moment, whether the body is still or moving.
screen: `WALKING AND SITTING, NAMED TOGETHER.` · `SITTING GOES DEEP, BUT CAN FADE.` · `WALKING WAKES, BUT CAN SCATTER.` · `SIT, WALK, SIT: THE RETREAT DAY.` · then, large: `TWO WAYS TO STAY.`

segments.voice: If there's room, stand and walk slowly for about a minute. Ten steps, turn, ten steps back. Lift, move, place. At the turn, pause and feel the whole body standing. Then come back to your seat and sit, and let the stillness arrive in a body that has just been moving. Notice the difference: the feet quiet now, the breath taking over as the thread. Later today, if you have ten minutes, try the full version: sit five, walk five. The bell holds the time.
Walking and sitting together. Two postures, one practice: sit until you fade, walk until you scatter, and come back to stillness again.
Your line: two ways to stay. Today, when you've been sitting too long and the mind goes foggy, get up and walk a slow minute. When you're scattered, sit. Day one hundred twenty-two.

howItsDone: On Buddhist meditation retreats the day often alternates periods of sitting with periods of slow walking meditation, and some practitioners at home walk for a few minutes between sittings.

match.prompt: match each piece of the walking week.
pairs: goes deep, but can slide into dullness
wakes the body, but can stay on the surface
lying down like a resting lion

myth: on retreat, walking periods are a rest from meditation
walking is meditation too: the old text names walking and sitting together as one practice.
the discourse on wakefulness has the monk walk and sit by day and in the first part of the night
he sleeps in the middle of the night, then walks and sits again before dawn.
you have to choose: some people are sitters, some are walkers
the point is to pair them, each covering the other's weak spot.

fork.setup: you've been sitting for forty minutes and your head keeps nodding. what does the retreat schedule suggest?
options: get up and walk for a while.
fork.reveal: walking wakes the body and clears dullness. then you sit again, and the stillness is easier to reach.

original.note: Pali: the postures (walking, standing, sitting, lying down), each one a place to practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: walking periods on retreat are just stretch breaks.
what it means: walking and sitting are one practice in two postures, each balancing the other.
what a scholar hears: the wakefulness passage (jagariyanuyoga) pairs walking back and forth and sitting for the day and the first and last watches of the night.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.16 (Apannaka Sutta), devotion to wakefulness
Majjhima Nikaya 53 (Sekha Sutta), the same wakefulness passage

notes: The wakefulness passage (walking and sitting by day, first and last watch; lying in the lion's posture in the middle watch) is paraphrased from AN 3.16 and MN 53; confirm the references.
Week-end look-back names days 117–121 (the lane, lifting-moving-placing, the turn, the five blessings, the city).
Dullness (thina-middha) is linked back to the hindrances taught on day 115.
Practice sized to a two-minute sit: a minute of walking, then sitting; the outline's 'sit five, walk five' is offered for later.
